{{Short description|Being present, not nothing}}
{{See also|Entity}}
'''Something''' and '''anything''' are [[concept]]s of [[existence]] in [[ontology]], contrasting with the concept of [[nothing]]. Both are used to describe the understanding that what exists is not [[nothing]] without needing to address the existence of [[everything]]. The [[Philosophy|philosopher]], [[David Lewis (philosopher)|David Lewis]], has pointed out that these are ''necessarily'' vague terms, asserting that "ontological assertions of common sense are correct if the quantifiers—such words as "something" and "anything"—are restricted roughly to ordinary or familiar things."<ref>Eli Hirsch, ''Quantifier Variance and Realism: Essays in Metaontology'' (2011), p. 106.</ref>

The idea that "something" is the opposite of "nothing" has existed at least since it was proposed by the [[Neoplatonism|Neoplatonist]] philosopher [[Porphyry (philosopher)|Porphyry]] in the 3rd century.<ref>[[Iamblichus]], ''Fragments of Iamblichus' Commentary on the Timaeus'', John Myles Dillon trans. (1973), p. 211.</ref> One of the most basic questions of both science and philosophy is: [[Why is there anything at all | why is there something rather than nothing at all?]]<ref>''See, e.g.'', Tyron Goldschmidt, ed., ''The Puzzle of Existence: Why Is There Something Rather Than Nothing?'' (2014).</ref> A question that follows from this is whether it is ever actually possible for there to be nothing at all, or whether there must always be something.<ref>''See, e.g.'', D. M. Armstrong, ''Truth and Truthmakers'' (2004), p. 89.</ref>

Grammatically, "''something'' and ''anything'' are commonly classified as [[pronoun]]s, although they do not stand for another noun so clearly as does ''[[object (philosophy)|thing]]'' itself, a word always classified as a noun".<ref>Robert Eustis Morsberger, Janet Rankin Aiken, ''Commonsense Grammar and Style'' (1975), p. 54.</ref>

==In predicate logic==
{{Main|Existential quantification}}
In [[predicate logic]], what is described in layman's terms as "something" can more specifically be regarded as [[existential quantification]], that is, the predication of a property or relation to at least one member of the domain. It is a type of [[Quantification (logic)|quantifier]], a [[logical constant]] which is [[interpretation (logic)|interpreted]] as "there exists," "there is at least one," or "for some." It expresses that a [[propositional function]] can be [[satisfiability|satisfied]] by at least one [[element (mathematics)|member]] of a [[domain of discourse]]. In other terms, it is the [[Predicate (mathematical logic)|predication]] of a [[property (philosophy)|property]] or [[binary relation|relation]]  to at least one member of the domain. It [[logical assertion|asserts]] that a predicate within the [[free variables and bound variables|scope]] of an existential quantifier is true of at least one [[Valuation (logic)|value]] of a [[predicate variable]].
